D01.title: What VS Code actually is
D01.text: VS Code is a text editor made for code. That is all. It does not run Python itself: it is the desk you work at, and Python is the worker. **Cursor** is a copy of VS Code with an AI helper built in, so every button you learn here works the same there. Learn one, know both.
D01.try: Open VS Code and find four areas: the icon strip on the far left, the big empty middle (the editor), the top menu, and the blue bar at the bottom. Just look. Change nothing.

D02.title: A project is a folder
D02.text: VS Code works on one **folder** at a time. Your files live in it and show in the left panel, called the **Explorer**. No folder open means VS Code does not know where your work is. Most beginner confusion is just this.
D02.try: Make a folder `Python 30 Work` in Documents. In VS Code click File, Open Folder, pick it, click Select Folder. Press Ctrl+Shift+E to show or hide the Explorer.

D03.title: New file, and why .py matters
D03.text: A Python program is a text file whose name ends in `.py`. The ending tells VS Code it is Python, so it colours your code and offers the Run button. Without `.py` it is treated as plain text and nothing helpful happens.
D03.try: In the Explorer, hover over your folder name and click the New File icon (a page with a plus). Name it `day3.py`, press Enter, and type `print(7 * 6)`. Watch the colours appear.

D04.title: The Run button and the terminal
D04.text: The triangle at the top right is **Run**. It opens a panel at the bottom called the **terminal** and tells Python to read your file. The long first line there is VS Code giving that order. Your output comes after it. The terminal is also where input() waits for you to type.
D04.try: Open `day3.py` and click the triangle. Read the bottom panel: skip the long line, find your output. Press Ctrl+` (the key under Esc) to hide and show the terminal.

D05.title: Saved or not saved
D05.text: Python runs the file on disk, not what you see on screen. A white dot on the file's tab means **not saved**, so Run would use the old version. Ctrl+S saves. Better: switch on Auto Save once and forget about it.
D05.try: Type something in `day3.py` and spot the dot on the tab. Press Ctrl+S and watch it go. Then click File and tick Auto Save.

D06.title: Indent with Tab
D06.text: You learned today that the 4 spaces matter. In VS Code the **Tab** key types those 4 spaces for you, and **Shift+Tab** takes them away. Select several lines first and Tab pushes them all in together. After a colon, VS Code even indents the next line by itself.
D06.try: Type an `if` line ending in a colon and press Enter: the cursor is already pushed in. Select two lines, press Tab, then Shift+Tab.

D07.title: Squiggles: errors before you run
D07.text: A red wavy line under your code is VS Code saying: Python will not be able to read this. It appears while you type, before you run. Hover the mouse over it to read why. All current problems are listed in the **Problems** panel.
D07.try: Delete a closing bracket in any file. Find the red squiggle, hover over it, then press Ctrl+Shift+M to open Problems. Put the bracket back and watch it clear.

D08.title: Stop a program that will not stop
D08.text: Today you met the endless loop. In the lesson page the app stops it for you. On your PC nothing does: it runs until you say stop. Click once inside the terminal and press **Ctrl+C**. If that fails, the bin icon on the terminal's right kills it.
D08.try: Make `loop.py` with `while True:` and an indented `print("still going")`. Run it, then click in the terminal and press Ctrl+C.

D09.title: Move, copy and mute a line
D09.text: Three keys that save retyping. **Alt+Up** or **Alt+Down** moves the line you are on. **Shift+Alt+Down** copies it below. **Ctrl+/** turns the line into a comment and back, which is how you switch a line off without deleting it.
D09.try: In any file with three print lines: move the bottom one to the top with Alt+Up, copy a line with Shift+Alt+Down, and mute one with Ctrl+/.

D10.title: The Command Palette
D10.text: You never need to remember which menu something is in. **Ctrl+Shift+P** opens the Command Palette: a search box for every single thing VS Code can do. Type a few letters of what you want and press Enter. It is the most useful key in the editor.
D10.try: Press Ctrl+Shift+P, type `theme`, choose Preferences: Color Theme, and arrow through a few. Pick one you like. Press Esc to close the palette any time.

D11.title: Autocomplete
D11.text: Type a list's name and a dot, and a menu appears with everything a list can do: `append`, `sort` and more. That menu is **autocomplete**. Arrow to one and press Tab or Enter to insert it. You do not have to remember spellings: let the editor offer them.
D11.try: Type `shots = ["wide"]` then on a new line type `shots.` and stop. Read the menu. Choose `append`. If the menu ever hides, press Ctrl+Space.

D12.title: Hover for help
D12.text: Rest the mouse on any Python word, such as `sorted` or `len`, and a small box explains what it does and what it needs. It is a pocket manual. Use it every time you meet a word you do not know, before you search the web.
D12.try: Type `print(sorted([3, 1, 2]))` and hold the mouse still over `sorted`. Read the first two lines of the box. Do the same on `print`.

D13.title: Find and replace
D13.text: **Ctrl+F** finds a word in the file and shows how many times it appears. **Ctrl+H** adds a second box to replace it. This is how you change a name that appears twenty times without missing one.
D13.try: In a file that uses a name several times, press Ctrl+F and type the name. Press Enter to jump between matches. Press Ctrl+H, type a new name, and click Replace All. Ctrl+Z undoes it.

D14.title: Many cursors at once
D14.text: Click on a word and press **Ctrl+D**: it selects the next copy of that word too, and now you type in both places at once. Press again for a third. **Alt+Click** puts an extra cursor anywhere. It looks like a trick but it is an everyday tool.
D14.try: Write three lines that each contain the word `take`. Click on the first, press Ctrl+D twice, and type `shot`. All three change together. Press Esc to go back to one cursor.

D15.title: Extensions: add-ons
D15.text: VS Code on its own knows very little about Python. The Run button, squiggles and autocomplete come from an **extension**: an add-on. The one you need is called Python, by Microsoft. Cursor uses the same extensions.
D15.try: Press Ctrl+Shift+X. Search `Python`. The one by Microsoft should say installed (a gear icon, no Install button). If it shows Install, click it. Install nothing else for now.

D16.title: Rename everywhere, jump to the source
D16.text: Now that you write functions: click on a function's name and press **F2** to rename it everywhere it is used, safely. Press **F12** on a call to jump to where that function is written. Alt+Left takes you back.
D16.try: Write a small function and call it twice. Click its name, press F2, type a better name, press Enter. Then click on a call and press F12.

D17.title: The debugger: pause your program
D17.text: A **breakpoint** tells Python: pause here. Click just left of a line number and a red dot appears. Press **F5** and choose Python File. The program stops at the dot, and the left panel shows every variable and its value right now. No more guessing.
D17.try: Put a red dot on a line inside one of your functions. Press F5, pick Python File. When it pauses, read the Variables list on the left. Press F5 again to let it finish.

D18.title: Step through line by line
D18.text: While paused at a breakpoint, **F10** runs exactly one line and pauses again. Watch the variables change as you go: it is your program in slow motion. **F5** carries on to the end, **Shift+F5** stops. This finds bugs faster than staring.
D18.try: Put a breakpoint on the first line of a loop. Press F5, then press F10 several times and watch the counter change in Variables. Shift+F5 to stop.

D19.title: Typing commands yourself
D19.text: The Run button only types a command into the terminal for you. You can type it yourself: `python hello.py`. Professionals mostly work this way. The **Up arrow** brings back your last command, `cls` wipes the screen, `dir` lists the files in the folder.
D19.try: Open the terminal with Ctrl+` and type `dir`, then `python hello.py` (use `py hello.py` if python is not found). Press Up arrow and Enter to run it again. Type `cls`.

D20.title: Jump between files, see two at once
D20.text: **Ctrl+P** opens a box: type part of a file name and press Enter to open it. Faster than clicking through folders. **Ctrl+\** splits the editor so two files sit side by side, handy for copying from an old program into a new one.
D20.try: Press Ctrl+P, type `hel`, press Enter to open hello.py. Press Ctrl+\ to split, then open a different file in the second half with Ctrl+P.

D21.title: Watch your program make files
D21.text: When your code writes a file, it appears in the Explorer straight away, and you can click it to read it. Right-click any file for Rename, Delete and **Reveal in File Explorer**, which opens the real Windows folder. The Explorer is just a window onto that folder.
D21.try: Run a tiny program that writes `note.txt`. Watch it appear on the left and click it. Right-click it, choose Reveal in File Explorer, then rename it from inside VS Code.

D22.title: Search the whole project
D22.text: Ctrl+F searches one file. **Ctrl+Shift+F** searches every file in the folder and lists each match with its line. When you think: where did I write that? this is the answer. Click a result to jump there.
D22.try: Press Ctrl+Shift+F and search for `print`. See how many files and lines it finds in your Python 30 Work folder. Click two results.

D23.title: Data files are just text
D23.text: A CSV opens in VS Code as plain text, and you see exactly what Python sees: commas and lines. Excel hides that. When a CSV program gives odd results, open the file in VS Code first: a stray space or an empty last line is usually the reason.
D23.try: Make `crew.csv` with a header line and two rows. Look at it in VS Code. Add a space after one comma and think about what your program would read.

D24.title: Make it yours: settings
D24.text: **Ctrl+,** opens Settings, with a search box at the top. Two worth changing: Font Size, so code is comfortable to read, and Word Wrap, so long lines do not run off the screen (**Alt+Z** toggles it). **Shift+Alt+F** tidies a messy JSON file.
D24.try: Press Ctrl+, and search `font size`: try 16. Open a JSON file, squash it onto one line, then press Shift+Alt+F. Toggle wrap with Alt+Z.

D25.title: One folder per project
D25.text: From now on each tool you build gets its own folder: the renamer in one, the invoice tool in another. Open that folder with File, Open Folder. **File, Open Recent** gets you back to any of them. This keeps tools apart, and Git (Day 28) needs it.
D25.try: Make a folder `renamer` inside Python 30 Work and open it with File, Open Folder. Then use File, Open Recent to return to Python 30 Work.

D26.title: Meet Cursor
D26.text: **Cursor** is VS Code with an AI assistant built in. Same Explorer, same terminal, same keys: everything from the last 25 days works there. It is free to download and use as an editor. The AI part has a limited free allowance and a paid plan for more. You do not need the plan to learn it. Prices change, so check cursor.com when you decide.
D26.try: Download Cursor from cursor.com and install it. On first start, accept the offer to import your VS Code settings and extensions. Open your Python 30 Work folder in it and run a file.

D27.title: Tab: the AI finishes your line
D27.text: As you type in Cursor, grey text may appear ahead of your cursor: the AI guessing what comes next. **Tab** accepts it, **Esc** or simply typing on rejects it. Rule for life: read it before you accept it. It is a guess, and you are the one who signs it off.
D27.try: In Cursor, start a function: type `def add_minutes(time, minutes):` and press Enter. If grey text appears, read it line by line. Accept with Tab only if you understand every line.

D28.title: Git with buttons
D28.text: The Git commands from today also live in a panel: **Ctrl+Shift+G** opens Source Control. Changed files are listed. Click one to see old and new side by side (a **diff**). Type a message and click Commit to make the save point. Same thing as the commands, just clicks.
D28.try: In your hello-git folder change one line, then press Ctrl+Shift+G. Click the changed file to see the diff. Type a message, click the plus to stage, then Commit.

D29.title: Ask the AI about your code
D29.text: Two keys in Cursor. **Ctrl+L** opens a chat beside your code: ask it to explain an error or a line. **Ctrl+K** edits in place: select some code, press it, and say what to change. The change shows as a diff you accept or reject. Best first use: explain this error in simple words.
D29.try: Open a program with a bug in Cursor. Run it, copy the error, press Ctrl+L and ask: explain this error simply, give me a hint, not the fix. Then fix it yourself.

D30.title: You direct, the AI assists
D30.text: Cursor's **Agent** (in the chat panel) can write and change whole files. It is fast and often wrong in small ways, so work like a director: ask for one small step, read every diff, run it, commit when it works, then ask for the next. You can do this now because you can read the code. Never paste passwords or keys into it.
D30.try: In Cursor, commit your invoice tool first. Then ask the Agent for one small change, such as: add a line that shows the number of crew. Read the diff, accept, run, commit.
